Correction (2026-08-16). WCL28's sessions on 9/11/23 and 9/13/23 were identified as contaminated and have been excluded from this cohort — that mouse now contributes 5 retrained sessions instead of 7, and the pooled cohort totals 39 sessions / 19,127 trials instead of the original 41 / 19,837. Every number, figure, and the WCL28-specific narrative below reflect the corrected data. The two contaminated sessions were driving a nonsensical pre-event interaction coefficient for WCL28 (+7.1, now a normal +0.08 in the corrected fit) and had exaggerated how much of an outlier WCL28 looked like in the paired comparison — see the rewritten subsection below.

Summary

One clean signal, one real dissociation, one contradiction worth sitting with

Five mice from the original FP1 “none” cohort were recorded again months later, after a training gap and an intervening DREADD/DCZ manipulation as part of a separate experiment. This is the only genuinely within-subject age comparison available in this dataset — each animal is its own control, which removes the between-animal confounds that limited the FP1-vs-FP2 comparison. It does not remove age from task re-experience or from that intervening pharmacological history, so it answers a related but different question than a clean age isolate would.

Of five pre-specified metrics compared original-vs-retrained, one shows a fully unanimous effect: signed-RPE's advantage over unsigned RPE shrank in all 5 mice (paired Wilcoxon p=0.0625, the best possible result obtainable at n=5). Two other metrics show partial, non-significant trends in opposite directions — the outcome×value interaction got numerically stronger in 4/5 mice, while overall encoding-model fit got numerically weaker in 4/5 mice. And the one unanimous result directly contradicts the (much weaker, non-significant) direction seen in the cross-sectional FP1-vs-FP2 comparison — a discrepancy discussed below rather than smoothed over.

What this design does and doesn't control for

Within-subject, but not a clean age isolate

Every confound that comes from comparing different animals (individual variability, viral batch, sex, baseline task ability) is removed by design — these are the same 5 mice, same implant, same fiber, compared to themselves. What isn't removed: between the two recordings, these mice underwent a DREADD/DCZ manipulation as part of a separate experiment, and had a training gap before being run again. The “none” condition still means no acute drug was on board during the sessions analyzed here (same definition used throughout this project), but the animals' history differs from a hypothetical mouse that simply aged untouched. Any difference below reflects age and task re-experience and possible lasting effects of that manipulation history, bundled together.

Two of the original 7 FP1 mice, WCL25 and WCL26, are not part of this retrained cohort — they were dropped from the study for reasons unrelated to this analysis, not because of anything in their data.

Retrained cohort, pooled models

The same reward-locked signal, reprocessed through the identical pipeline

Hemisphere for these sessions wasn't available from a prior MATLAB channel scan, so it was supplied directly: channel 5 (green_l) throughout, consistent with sessions recorded well after the rig's known mid-2023 channel cutover. Four of the five mice (WCL23, 24, 27, 29) show a hemisphere change from their original recording (all were green_r then); WCL28 was already green_l both times. This is the known hardware cutover, not a biological change, and both recordings are still resolved to their own correct channel.

Both models reproduce the same qualitative shape seen in every cohort analyzed so far: a sharp, reward-locked step at the event, smooth reward-history ramps with no discontinuity at t=0, and FIR kernels that separate cleanly by recent-outcome history. The retraining/aging process did not disrupt the basic encoding architecture.

A dissociation worth naming, not averaging away

The interaction coefficient (a specific value-modulation effect) got numerically stronger in 4 of 5 mice after retraining, while the encoding model's overall peak R² (how much of the signal's variance the whole model explains) got numerically weaker in 4 of 5 mice — nearly the same 4 mice in both cases, but moving in opposite directions. One plausible reading: the specific outcome×value effect sharpened, while something else (background noise, signal quality, or a general drop in explanatory power from longer-term implant/expression changes common in chronic fiber photometry) pulled overall model fit down independently. This is a description of the pattern, not a resolved mechanism — with n=5, it should be treated as a lead worth checking against the raw session-overview figures, not a settled conclusion.

WCL28 is still the one exception on the interaction coefficient — but only that, not a two-metric pattern

With the two contaminated sessions removed, WCL28 remains the one mouse whose interaction coefficient moved opposite the other four (weaker, not stronger, after retraining: −1.271 → −0.874) and its βRPE still flattens the most of the five (−0.560 → −0.129, again nearly to zero). Both of those hold up after the correction, just less dramatically than the contaminated data suggested (interaction was previously read as reversing almost to zero at −0.603; it's actually a smaller, though still real, weakening to −0.874). What does not hold up: WCL28's FIR out-of-sample R² was previously the one mouse declining alongside a supposed two-metric divergence — corrected, it actually improves slightly (0.168 → 0.170), same direction as the majority. So WCL28 is an outlier on one metric (the interaction coefficient), not two related ones as the contaminated data implied. That's a real, narrower finding, not a data-quality artifact — but it no longer supports a story about this mouse diverging across the board.

Comparing against the cross-sectional result

The one unanimous finding here contradicts the FP1-vs-FP2 comparison

The FP1-vs-FP2 report found signed-RPE's advantage over unsigned RPE trending upward with age — FP1 (young) median 0.014 vs. FP2 (old) median 0.088, not significant (p=0.23), and itself driven unevenly by only 2 of FP2's 4 mice (WCL30=0.222, WCL33=0.141, vs. WCL31=−0.016 and WCL32=0.034). This within-subject comparison finds the opposite: the same metric declining from 0.014 to −0.011, and doing so in every one of the 5 mice tested — a far more consistent signal than the cross-sectional one, just pointing the other way.

This is a genuine discrepancy, not a rounding difference. Two honest explanations compete: (1) both results are small-n noise and neither reflects a real, stable age effect on this metric; or (2) the retrained cohort's added confounds — the intervening DREADD/DCZ history and task re-experience, absent from FP2's naturally-old mice — are doing something to this specific measure that plain chronological age does not. The data here cannot distinguish these two explanations. What can be said is that the within-subject result, despite being the numerically cleaner one (unanimous vs. 2-of-4), should not be read as the more valid characterization of “the age effect” on this metric — it is a characterization of an aged-and-manipulated mouse, which is a different, narrower thing.

Interpretation

What carries forward, and what doesn't

The core reward-locked encoding survives retraining/aging intact in both pooled models, at a magnitude close to the original cohort's. The within-subject comparison adds one specific, well-powered-for-its-n finding — a unanimous decline in the signed-RPE advantage — alongside two weaker, non-significant trends (interaction strengthening, overall fit weakening) that together describe a plausible but unresolved dissociation between a sharpening specific effect and a declining general one. None of this should be read as settling the age question raised by the FP1-vs-FP2 comparison: that comparison and this one disagree on the one metric both could speak to, and the honest reading is that this cohort's added confounds (DREADD history, task re-experience) make it a different experiment from a pure age contrast, not a cleaner version of the same one.

Scope. n=5 pairs caps this analysis at a paired-Wilcoxon floor of p=0.0625 even for a fully unanimous result — only the ΔR² metric reached that floor here. WCL25/WCL26's absence from this cohort is a fact about the study, not evidence about their task learning. The DREADD/DCZ history between recordings is a first-order confound for any age-effect claim from this specific comparison.
